intro: Sorting and binary search are the two workhorse techniques that unlock a huge fraction of competitive-programming and placement-exam problems: sorting imposes structure you can exploit (monotonicity, grouping, order statistics), and binary search exploits that structure to cut search spaces from O(n) to O(log n). The most powerful application, binary search on the answer, generalizes the idea from "find a value in a sorted array" to "find the optimal value of any monotonic feasibility predicate," turning otherwise intractable optimization problems into a handful of feasibility checks.

subtopics.name: Sorting Algorithm Tradeoffs
subtopics.theory:
Every comparison-based sort is bounded below by Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, so the interesting differences between quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort are not about their average-case time complexity (all three are O(n log n) on average) but about stability, worst-case guarantees, memory usage, and constant factors. Quicksort (what std::sort typically uses, blended with introsort/heapsort fallback and insertion sort for small partitions) has excellent cache locality and the best practical constant factor, but a naive implementation is O(n^2) worst case on adversarial or already-sorted input; production implementations defend against this with random pivots, median-of-three pivots, or by switching to heapsort after too many recursion levels (introsort, which is what the C++ standard mandates for std::sort's worst-case bound). Quicksort is also NOT stable: equal elements can be reordered relative to each other.

Mergesort is stable (equal elements keep their relative input order) and has a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case, which matters when input can be adversarial or when stability is required (e.g., sorting by a secondary key after already sorting by a primary key). The cost is O(n) auxiliary space for the merge step and generally worse cache behavior / constant factor than quicksort on random data. std::stable_sort is typically an implementation of mergesort for this reason. Heapsort is in-place (O(1) extra space) with a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case, but it is not stable and has poor cache locality because of its access pattern jumping around the heap array, making it slower in practice than quicksort or mergesort despite the same asymptotic complexity; it is mainly useful as the 'safety net' fallback that gives introsort its worst-case guarantee, and as the engine behind priority queues and heap-based algorithms (Dijkstra, k-way merges).

When array elements come from a small, bounded domain (e.g., integers in [0, k) with k = O(n)), non-comparison sorts break the Omega(n log n) lower bound entirely: counting sort runs in O(n + k) and is naturally stable when implemented with a prefix-sum placement pass, and radix sort applies counting sort digit-by-digit to sort O(n) w-bit integers in O(n * w / log n) time. Recognizing that problem constraints put values in a small range (say, sorting 10^6 integers each at most 10^5) is a classic signal to reach for counting sort instead of std::sort, saving a log factor.

In competitive programming you almost never hand-implement quicksort/mergesort/heapsort; the actual skill being tested is (1) choosing stable vs unstable sort correctly when a problem has a hidden secondary ordering requirement, (2) writing correct custom comparators (especially ones that must form a valid strict-weak-ordering, e.g., the 'concatenation' comparator for largest-number problems), and (3) recognizing when bounded-value constraints allow you to drop to a faster non-comparison sort.
subtopics.recognition: Reach for this topic's ideas when: a problem asks you to arrange/reorder elements under a custom rule that is not plain numeric order (needs a custom comparator, and you must argue it is a valid total order); a problem's correctness depends on ties preserving original order (stability); or the input values are bounded by something small relative to n, hinting that O(n + k) counting/radix sort beats O(n log n) comparison sort. If a solution's correctness argument breaks when two equal elements swap places, you need a stable sort or an explicit tie-breaker (e.g., include the original index as a secondary sort key).
subtopics.complexity: Quicksort (introsort/std::sort): O(n log n) average and (with introsort fallback) worst case, O(log n) extra space for recursion, NOT stable. Mergesort/std::stable_sort: O(n log n) worst case guaranteed, O(n) extra space, stable. Heapsort: O(n log n) worst case guaranteed, O(1) extra space, NOT stable. Counting/radix sort: O(n + k) / O(n * w/log n), O(n + k) extra space, stable if implemented via prefix sums.

examples.title: Largest Number (custom comparator)
examples.problem: Given n non-negative integers, arrange them (each used exactly once) so that their decimal concatenation forms the largest possible number, and print that number as a string (with no leading zeros, unless the result is exactly "0"). Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= a[i] <= 10^9.
examples.approach: This is not orderable by plain numeric or lexicographic comparison of the numbers themselves (e.g., 9 should come before 30 even though '30' < '9' lexicographically as a prefix issue). Convert every number to its decimal string, then sort the strings with the comparator cmp(a, b) := (a+b) > (b+a) as strings, i.e., a should precede b iff placing a first yields a lexicographically larger concatenation. This comparator is provably a valid strict weak ordering (transitivity follows from comparing digit blocks), so std::sort with it produces a correct total order. After sorting, concatenate all strings; finally, strip leading zeros (but keep a single '0' if every element was zero).

examples.title: Ranking Students (stability matters)
examples.problem: You are given n students in input order, each with a name and an integer score. Print the students sorted by score in descending order; students with equal scores must keep their original relative (input) order. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000, 0 <= score <= 100.
examples.approach: This is the canonical demonstration of why stability matters: sorting only by 'score descending' does not fully specify the output when scores tie, so the algorithm must preserve input order among equal elements. Using std::sort here is unsafe because it is not guaranteed stable (equal elements may be reordered arbitrarily by its internal introsort). The correct tool is std::stable_sort with the comparator only comparing score (descending); stable_sort guarantees O(n log^2 n) worst case (O(n log n) with enough extra memory, which is the common case) and never disturbs the relative order of elements that compare equal. An equivalent alternative that also works with plain sort is to break ties explicitly by original index.

subtopics.name: Binary Search
subtopics.theory:
Classic binary search finds a target (or a boundary) inside a structure with a monotonic order in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search interval [lo, hi]. The essential invariant to keep in your head is not 'the array is sorted' but 'the predicate I'm testing at each midpoint is monotonic over the search range' — sortedness is just the most common way that monotonicity arises. At each step you evaluate the predicate at mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 (never (lo + hi) / 2, to avoid signed overflow on large indices) and discard the half of the range that cannot contain the answer. The two most common templates are: (1) exact-match search, shrinking until lo > hi or the element is found; and (2) boundary search (as in std::lower_bound / std::upper_bound), which finds the first index where a predicate flips from false to true, using a loop of the form while (lo < hi) { mid = ...; if (pred(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1; }.

A large family of 'hard' binary search problems apply the technique to structures that are only piecewise sorted or sorted along a derived quantity rather than the raw array: searching a rotated sorted array (the array is sorted except for one rotation point, and at every step exactly one half of any sub-range is guaranteed properly sorted, which is enough information to decide which half to recurse into), or binary searching over a partition index into two arrays to find a median without merging them. These problems are 'binary search' in the sense that the state space, not necessarily the raw array, is monotonic — the discipline is to precisely state the invariant you're maintaining and prove it holds after each halving step, since off-by-one errors are the single most common source of bugs in this topic.

It's worth internalizing why binary search is provably optimal for plain search in a sorted array: any comparison-based search algorithm needs Omega(log n) comparisons in the worst case (an adversary argument / decision-tree lower bound), and binary search matches that bound exactly.
subtopics.recognition: Use classic binary search when the data is sorted (or can be sorted up front cheaply) and you need membership, insertion position, or a boundary/count query in O(log n); when the phrase 'find the first/last index such that...' appears; or when a structure is 'almost sorted' in a way that still lets you determine, from O(1) probes at the midpoint, which half must contain the answer (rotated arrays, bitonic arrays, or a derived monotonic quantity like a partition balance in the two-sorted-array median problem).
subtopics.complexity: O(log n) time per search, O(1) extra space (iterative) or O(log n) stack space (recursive).

examples.title: Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
examples.problem: An array of n distinct integers, originally sorted in ascending order, has been rotated at some unknown pivot (e.g., [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] rotated at index 3 becomes [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Given the rotated array and a target value, return the index of the target, or -1 if it is not present. Must run in O(log n) time. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 5000, all elements distinct.
examples.approach: At any midpoint, even though the whole array isn't sorted, at least one of the two halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] IS a contiguous sorted run (rotation can only break sortedness at one point). So at each step: compare a[lo] with a[mid] to determine which half is properly sorted; then check whether the target lies within that sorted half's value range. If it does, recurse into that half; otherwise the target (if present) must be in the other half. This keeps the search space halving every step, giving O(log n).

examples.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
examples.problem: Given two sorted arrays nums1 (size m) and nums2 (size n), find the median of the combined sorted array in O(log(min(m, n))) time (merging, which is O(m+n), is too slow for the intended constraints m, n up to 10^6). Print the median with 5 digits after the decimal point.
examples.approach: Binary search over a partition index i in the smaller array (WLOG size m <= n). For a given i, the mirrored partition in the other array is forced: j = (m + n + 1) / 2 - i, so that the left side of the combined partition has exactly ceil((m+n)/2) elements. A partition is correct when max(left side of A) <= min(right side of B) AND max(left side of B) <= min(right side of A); if the first condition fails (A's left is too large), shrink i; if the second fails, grow i. When a valid partition is found, the median is either max(leftA, leftB) (odd total length) or the average of max(leftA, leftB) and min(rightA, rightB) (even total length). Sentinels INT_MIN/INT_MAX handle empty partitions cleanly.

subtopics.name: Binary Search on the Answer
subtopics.theory:
Binary search on the answer (a.k.a. 'binary search over the value space') is used when you cannot compute the optimal answer directly, but you CAN cheaply check, for a fixed candidate answer x, whether x is 'feasible' (e.g., 'can we achieve at least this much', or 'can we finish within this much time/cost'), and feasibility is monotonic in x. If feasible(x) is monotonic — every x' >= x is also feasible whenever x is (or the symmetric case for minimizing) — then the set of feasible x forms a contiguous suffix (or prefix) of the value line, and you can binary search for the boundary between infeasible and feasible exactly like std::lower_bound, except the 'array' is implicit: it's the predicate feasible(mid), evaluated on demand instead of read from memory.

The template for minimizing an answer is: lo = smallest conceivable value, hi = largest conceivable value (a safe upper bound, often derivable from a trivial feasible construction); while (lo < hi) { mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if (feasible(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1; }; answer = lo. Maximizing is the mirror image with feasible(mid) shrinking lo upward. The entire complexity of the algorithm collapses into two parts: (1) proving monotonicity (often the 'aha' insight — it is rarely stated in the problem and must be argued informally, e.g. 'if we can pack everything using capacity x, we can certainly pack it using any larger capacity'), and (2) designing an efficient feasibility check, which is frequently a greedy linear scan, a two-pointer count, or a difference-array / prefix-sum computation.

This technique is what separates 'medium' from 'hard' binary search problems: the binary search itself is boilerplate, but recognizing that a problem phrased as 'minimize the maximum X' or 'maximize the minimum Y' or 'find the smallest T such that...' is secretly a monotonic feasibility problem — rather than something requiring direct DP or a closed-form formula — is the actual skill. A huge number of CP problems ('minimize the largest subarray sum when splitting into k pieces', 'maximize the minimum distance between placed items', 'find the k-th smallest pairwise distance') reduce to exactly this pattern.
subtopics.recognition: Strong signals: the problem says 'minimize the maximum ...' or 'maximize the minimum ...'; it asks for the smallest/largest value of some quantity such that a condition holds, and directly computing that value seems to require trying all possibilities; and you can write (even if slowly) a function feasible(x) that tells you in O(n) or O(n log n) whether a candidate value x works, and you can convince yourself that feasibility only turns on (never off) as x increases (or vice versa).
subtopics.complexity: O(log(range) * feasibility-check-cost). Feasibility checks are typically O(n) (greedy scan) or O(n log n) (two-pointer over a sorted array, or a scan needing a sort up front), giving overall O(n log(range)) or O(n log n log(range)).

examples.title: Factory Machines
examples.problem: There are k machines producing identical products; machine i needs t_i seconds to make one product, and all machines work in parallel and continuously (machine i can produce floor(T / t_i) products in T seconds). Find the minimum number of seconds T needed so that the machines together have produced at least n products in total. Constraints: 1 <= k <= 2*10^5, 1 <= n <= 10^9, 1 <= t_i <= 10^9. (CSES 1620, Factory Machines.)
examples.approach: Computing the optimal T directly is hard because production is a sum of floor divisions with different rates. But feasibility is trivial to check and monotonic: for a fixed candidate time T, the total products made is sum(floor(T / t_i)) over all machines, an O(k) computation, and this total is clearly non-decreasing as T grows. So binary search T over [1, huge upper bound] (e.g., up to n * max(t_i), or just a very large constant since t_i, n <= ~10^9), and find the smallest T with total production >= n.

examples.title: Array Division (minimize the maximum subarray sum)
examples.problem: Given an array of n positive integers, divide it into k contiguous, non-empty subarrays so as to minimize the largest sum among the k subarrays. Print that minimized maximum sum. Constraints: 1 <= k <= n <= 2*10^5, 1 <= a_i <= 10^9. (CSES 1085, Array Division; equivalent to LeetCode's Split Array Largest Sum.)
examples.approach: Binary search on the candidate maximum sum M. Feasibility check: greedily scan the array left to right, accumulating a running sum for the current subarray; whenever adding the next element would exceed M, start a new subarray there instead. Count how many subarrays this greedy scan needs; if that count is <= k, M is feasible (we can always merge extra small pieces together without exceeding M, or simply use fewer than k cuts). Feasibility is monotonic in M (a larger cap can only need fewer or equal subarrays), so binary search between lo = max single element (a lower bound, since that element alone must fit in some subarray) and hi = total sum (trivially feasible with 1 subarray) finds the minimum feasible M.

examples.title: K-th Smallest Pair Distance
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers, define the distance of a pair (i, j) with i < j as |nums[i] - nums[j]|. Find the k-th smallest such distance among all C(n,2) pairs. Constraints: 2 <= n <= 10^4, 1 <= k <= n*(n-1)/2, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^6. (LeetCode 719.)
examples.approach: Sort the array. Binary search on the candidate distance d in [0, max-min]. The feasibility check counts how many pairs have distance <= d: after sorting, use a two-pointer sliding window — for each right endpoint, advance left while a[right]-a[left] > d, then every index between left and right (inclusive on the left side) pairs with right at distance <= d, contributing (right - left) pairs; summing this over all right endpoints is an O(n) pass (each pointer moves forward only). This count is monotonic non-decreasing in d, so binary search for the smallest d with count(d) >= k gives exactly the k-th smallest pair distance.
